strengths: Addresses a practically important problem in LLM evaluation with clear motivation and compelling illustrations of bias direction and magnitude
Mathematically sound approach building on classical prevalence estimation with rigorous derivations; proofs of Propositions 1-2 are correct
Novel and complete treatment: derives confidence intervals accounting for uncertainty from both test and calibration datasets, addressing a gap in prior work
Practical contribution: adaptive allocation algorithm (Algorithm 1) provides concrete guidance for efficient calibration design with demonstrated efficiency gains (Figure 4c)
Comprehensive empirical validation through 16+ Monte Carlo scenarios with 10,000 replications each, consistently validating theory across diverse parameter configurations
Reproducible: simple Python implementation provided, clear experimental specifications, well-structured appendices with extensive supplementary results
Clear presentation with logical progression and effective visualizations; the paper is well-written and accessible
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core bias-correction formula is from Rogan & Gladen (1978); main contributions are applying existing methods to LLM evaluation and deriving CIs, both somewhat incremental

Critically lacks real-world empirical validation: all experiments are synthetic Monte Carlo simulations. No case studies with actual LLM judges (GPT-4, Claude) on real evaluation tasks limits practical impact demonstration

Theoretical assumptions are restrictive and under-discussed: Proposition 1 requires m₀=m₁ and q₀=q₁; Proposition 2 requires q̃₀, q̃₁ 'close to 1' without clear definition; impact of violations not explored

Insufficient practical guidance: missing discussion on obtaining calibration ground-truth at scale, handling judge drift over time, sensitivity to pilot size m_pilot, test vs. calibration budget tradeoffs, and clipping behavior
No comparison to alternative approaches: doesn't compare to other bias-correction schemes, Bayesian methods, or prediction-powered inference; no robustness analysis when q₀, q₁ are misspecified
Compressed presentation of theory: Section 4 is brief; Proposition 1's condition m ≳ q/(2q-1)² lacks intuitive explanation; the d_θ̃ term appears without sufficient motivation
Limited scope of adaptive allocation: only addresses m₀ vs. m₁ tradeoff, not n vs. (m₀+m₁) or more complex evaluation scenarios
Edge case handling not addressed: behavior when q₀ + q₁ < 1 (undefined adjustment), truncation effects on coverage, sufficient calibration sizes for practical use remain unclear

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: bias in LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation that could systematically distort reported model improvements
Sound mathematical framework with rigorous proofs: correct bias analysis, proper derivation of adjusted estimator and confidence intervals using delta method and adjusted Wald approach
Complete statistical treatment: uniquely accounts for uncertainty from both test and calibration datasets, unlike prior work focused only on point estimation
Novel practical contribution: adaptive allocation algorithm (Proposition 2, Algorithm 1) efficiently allocates calibration resources with clear theoretical optimality guarantees
Excellent presentation: clear exposition, intuitive figures (especially Fig. 1-2), logical flow from motivation to methods to validation
Comprehensive empirical validation: extensive Monte Carlo simulations across 16 parameter configurations with 10,000 replications each, with results in main paper and appendix
Practical accessibility: working Python code implementation provided, making adoption straightforward for practitioners
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core bias correction simply applies classical Rogan-Gladen (1978) estimator; while timely, the statistical techniques are not new
No real-world validation: relies entirely on synthetic Monte Carlo simulations; missing empirical evaluation on actual LLM judgments against human ground truth (e.g., on benchmarks like MTBench)
Restricted scope: limited to binary classification (correct/incorrect); no treatment of multi-class, soft labels, or regression settings common in practice
Theoretical assumptions not fully explored: Proposition 1 assumes symmetric case (m₀=m₁, q₀=q₁); behavior near boundary q₀+q₁=1 and with asymmetric allocations understudied

Limited practical guidance: paper doesn't specify when bias correction matters in practice (e.g., bias magnitude thresholds), how to choose calibration sizes without prior knowledge of q₀, q₁, or how to handle real-world distribution shifts
Missing real-world application example: would benefit from concrete case study before methods section showing the problem on actual data
Incomplete technical details: code repository link appears placeholder ('available at'), no discussion of numerical stability near denominator boundaries or edge case handling

strengths: Addresses a critical and timely practical problem: bias in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation that could mislead the field
Rigorous theoretical framework with complete proofs, properly applying delta method for confidence intervals accounting for both test and calibration dataset uncertainty

Comprehensive experimental validation through extensive Monte Carlo simulations (multiple parameter configurations) and real-world Chatbot Arena experiments with proper coverage probability verification
Valuable insights including characterization of when LLM evaluation outperforms human evaluation (Section 6) and robustness to distribution shift (Section 7) compared to alternatives
Practical accessibility: simple plug-in method with provided Python code that operates on existing scores; adaptive allocation strategy (Algorithm 1) reduces calibration requirements
Clear presentation with effective motivation, logical progression, good visualizations, and accessible writing that makes principled statistical practice understandable to ML practitioners
Complete methodological package: bias correction + confidence intervals + optimal calibration allocation provides a comprehensive solution
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution directly applies classical Rogan & Gladen (1978) method to new domain; extensions (standard Wald CI, straightforward optimization) are incremental

Practical limitations significantly restrict applicability: requires human-annotated calibration dataset, reducing advantage of LLM evaluation; conditions for LLM superiority are restrictive (q≥0.854, θ≈0.5)

Strong distributional assumptions not fully justified: assumes Pr(Ẑ|Z) invariant across datasets; real violations (domain shift, prompt changes, LLM updates) could invalidate results; handling auxiliary factors ξ left as future work

Insufficient practical guidance: unclear minimum calibration set size heuristics; limited analysis of when Proposition 5.2's assumption 'q₀ and q₁ close to 1' holds; sensitivity to pilot sample size not explored
Limited experimental scope: Chatbot Arena validation uses single judge (GPT-4.1-mini); no comparison with recent bias correction alternatives; binary classification only

Incomplete failure case analysis: numerical stability when q₀+q₁≈1; performance with very small calibration sets (m<20); highly imbalanced true labels; effect of center adjustment in Eq. (8) not quantified
Presentation could improve: heavy notation (tildes in Eq. 7); medical statistics terminology may not be clear to ML audience; missing discussion of multi-class evaluation and model drift detection

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: bias in LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, directly relevant to current ML evaluation practices
Novel theoretical contribution on robustness to distribution shift (Section 8): shows the proposed method remains unbiased when Pr(Z)≠Pr_Q(Z), distinguishing it from PPI and other methods

Comprehensive empirical validation: extensive Monte Carlo simulations across multiple configurations with consistent 95% coverage, real-world validation on Chatbot Arena, and multiple parameter regimes tested
Practical utility: simple plug-in method with provided Python code, actionable Algorithm 1 for adaptive calibration allocation, clear guidance on minimal calibration budgets
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Figure 2 clearly illustrates the bias problem, well-motivated problem formulation in Section 3, and logical flow through methodology

Rigorous theoretical framework: proper variance derivation using delta method accounting for both test and calibration uncertainty, optimal allocation result (Proposition 5.2), and analysis of parameter regimes for LLM vs. human-only evaluation
weaknesses: Limited core methodological novelty: the bias-correction formula (Eq. 5) is directly from Rogan & Gladen (1978), and variance derivation uses standard delta method. Primary contribution is applying 46-year-old epidemiology techniques to a new domain rather than developing new theory

Restrictive theoretical assumptions reduce practical applicability: Proposition 5.1 assumes equal label counts (m=2m₀=2m₁) and equal sensitivity/specificity (q₀=q₁); 'sufficiently large m' requirement lacks practical interpretation with no guidance on convergence rates

Missing empirical comparison with main competing method: no direct comparison with Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) on the same real-world datasets despite claiming advantages; distribution shift comparison in Figure 7 uses only synthetic data with uniform variation, not realistic distributional shifts

Narrow practical parameter regimes: Section 6 shows LLM-as-a-judge is preferable primarily near θ=0.5 and requires n→∞; practitioners cannot know true θ in advance, limiting actionability of Proposition 6.1

Limited real-world evaluation scope: Chatbot Arena validation uses only 6 models, single LLM judge (GPT-4.1-mini), and 10% calibration split; generalization to other judges and evaluation settings unclear; human labeling protocol not fully described

Incomplete analysis of failure modes and edge cases: no discussion of behavior when q̂₀+q̂₁→1 (singular denominator in Eq. 5), adversarially biased judges, or confounded judgments; Algorithm 1 uses m_pilot=10 without justification or sensitivity analysis
Reproducibility concerns: promised code URL is redacted in appendix; exact prompting strategy for LLM judge not specified; lack of details on inter-annotator agreement for Chatbot Arena labels

Unstated quantitative bounds on key assumptions: Proposition 5.2 requires q₀ and q₁ 'close to 1' without quantification; confidence interval uses adjusted Wald approach without discussing when this breaks down vs. alternatives like score-based intervals

strengths: Addresses a critical practical problem in LLM evaluation that affects reproducibility and reporting across ML research

Rigorous theoretical analysis including unbiasedness results, optimal allocation strategy (Proposition 5.2), and important distribution shift robustness result that prior methods like PPI lack (Section 8, Figure 8)
Comprehensive empirical validation with extensive Monte Carlo simulations across parameter ranges, real-world benchmarks (Chatbot Arena, AlpacaEval), and proper coverage analysis

Practical contributions including simple plug-in Python implementation, adaptive calibration allocation algorithm with theoretical optimality guarantees, and clear guidance on calibration budget requirements
Excellent reproducibility with detailed appendices, experimental setups, proofs, and provided code
Well-written presentation with effective illustrations clearly conveying main ideas; extends to multi-category evaluations
weaknesses: Limited core methodological novelty: the bias-corrected estimator (Eq. 5) and confidence interval construction directly apply Rogan & Gladen (1978) and Lang & Reiczigel (2014); the novel contribution is primarily application to LLMs rather than new statistical methods

Critical practical limitation: Figure 6 shows that current LLM judges do NOT fall in the favorable parameter regime on Chatbot Arena where the method reduces variance compared to human-only evaluation—undermining the practical motivation since calibration requires human annotation anyway
Invariance assumption Pr_P(Ẑ|Z) = Pr_Q(Ẑ|Z) may be violated by nuisance factors (response length, style); this vulnerability is acknowledged but not experimentally evaluated
Limited real-world evaluation scope: only two benchmarks tested, both involving pairwise preferences; broader evaluation tasks would strengthen applicability claims

Insufficient treatment of practical tradeoffs: comparison with PPI's variance reduction vs. bias robustness is incomplete; guidance on when practitioners should prefer this method over alternatives is unclear
Finite-sample behavior of confidence intervals relies on asymptotics and ad-hoc 'add two' adjustment; edge case coverage (θ near 0 or 1) could be analyzed more rigorously

Multi-category extension (Appendix B) is underdeveloped for practical use—requiring additional structure on confusion matrices for stability, but main text doesn't emphasize these practical challenges
